Consult Summary:
- Telehealth consult for 3-day acute diarrhea (4–5/day) with mild abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting; no blood or mucus; appears hydrated. Conservative management and safety-net advice provided.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Diarrhea for ~3 days, occurring 4–5 times/day; consistency varies from watery to loose depending on time of day.
- Associated symptoms: Mild abdominal pain; one episode of vomiting; decreased appetite; possible mild fever (“maybe a little bit”); able to maintain oral fluids.
- Pertinent negatives: No blood or mucus in stool. No recent travel. No concerning/“dodgy” food exposures reported.
- Past medical history: Asthma.
- Medications: Patient reports using an inhaler; name stated as “Lexapro” (doctor heard “Laxepro”); yellow inhaler—identity unclear; dose/route/frequency not documented. No other medications reported. No OTC taken for current symptoms.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Father had hypertension and died of bowel cancer at age 62 (~10 years ago).
- Social history/preventive: Not discussed.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Findings: Via video, clinician noted patient “looks not dehydrated.” Patient reports drinking adequate fluids.

Impression:
- Acute diarrhea without red-flag features currently; tolerating fluids.

Plan:
- Hydration: Increase fluids; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) to replace salts and fluids.
- Diet: Follow a “soft” diet—crackers, toast, jam; then add boiled/mashed vegetables. Avoid milk, fish, meat, and eggs while symptomatic. Yogurt/probiotics acceptable. After 48 hours without diarrhea, gradually reintroduce meat/eggs/fish.
- Medications: None started; OTC oral rehydration recommended.
- Safety net:
  - Seek care if stool frequency increases significantly (thresholds discussed as “>8/day” versus “about 6–8/day”—see conflict noted), signs of dehydration develop, or inability to keep fluids down.
  - Provide a stool sample if diarrhea persists beyond 1 week or if blood appears in stool (possible need for antibiotics depending on results).
  - Contact the clinic or seek hospital care if worsening as above.
- Follow-up: Return if symptoms persist >1 week, worsen, or red-flag features develop.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements:
  - Exact medication reconciliation (inhaler identity, doses, routes, frequencies) incomplete.
  - No vitals obtained.
  - No detailed review of systems beyond GI and constitutional symptoms.
  - Social history (smoking, alcohol), surgical history not discussed.
● Internal conflicts:
  - Stool-frequency threshold for concern stated as “>8/day” earlier and later as “about 6–8/day” for possible dehydration/hospital evaluation (conflict noted).
  - Inhaler name reported variably as “Lexapro” (patient) vs “Laxepro” (clinician); identity unclear.
● Transcript quality:
  - Occasional unclear audio/phrasing (e.g., “Mostly it’s been dry and red” — context unclear). Overall adequate to capture key clinical details.
